newsitem.title: CHILE: Copper--Chile's Refimet smelter plans expansion.
newsitem.headline: Copper--Chile's Refimet smelter plans expansion.

text.p: Chilean copper smelter Refimet, fresh from a major expansion, plans to boost output still more to handle up to 680,000 tonnes of concentrates a year by 1999 from 450,000 tonnes now, president Alfonso Dulanto said.

Refimet, which buys copper concentrates with a metal grade of about 35 percent and turns them into blister and cathodes, plans to spend about $100 million on the expansion at its complex outside Antofagasta.
"Right now we're discussing where to get the money or the partners," Dulanto told Reuters in an interview. "But we're expanding no matter what."
The company is owned 50.1 percent by Chilean group Inversiones del Pacifico SA, 25.1 percent by Barrick Gold Corp and the rest by Noranda Inc.
"Our plan is to widen our concentrate processing capacity from 450,000 tonnes to about 680,000 tonnes, which means an investment of about $100 million," Dulanto said.
In fine copper terms, the company's capacity is now at about 180,000 tonnes a year following a $60 million investment in 1996.

Refimet's board will meet in late July to decide on which way to go for financing the expansion, Dulanto said. Noranda has expressed interest in taking a larger profile in the stock participation, one possible way to finance the expansion, and metal trading companies and foreign refineries are also being considered, he said.
"They're all potential partners in the international mining sector," Dulanto said. In any case, the Chilean owners don't have the same easy access to credit as the Canadians do, he said.

Part of the expansion plan is "to change drastically in our technology, to one which is more efficient, modern and environmentally clean," he said. The plant's smoke emissions can be seen for miles around in northern Chile's Atacama desert.
Private copper mines Escondida, owned by BHP, and Mantos Blancos are the main suppliers of concentrates to Refimet, as well as local company Cascada.
Part of the finished product is sold to Codelco, but most is exported straight to Japan, South Korea or Europe, he said.

He said Refimet's aim is to keep ahead of rivals reported to be positioning for a push into Chile's growing metals smelting and refining industry, including Hyundai CORP and electricity generator Endesa.
"The smelting capacity that we plan by 1999 will be up and running by the time any of those projects becomes a reality," said Dulanto.
Although the parent company Inversiones del Pacifico may someday place shares on the Santiago exchange, Refimet has no plans to do so to finance the expansion.

"Both Noranda and Barrick Gold have enough resources on their own to contribute their share of their financing needed for expanding the capacity of the company, without placing shares on the bolsa," he said.
